scenario_stem:
Wexcombe Pottery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 12 years ago and employing 58 workers at its Stokeham workshop. Staff belong to the Clay & Ceramics Union, which has tabled a 6% pay claim after the published final accounts showed revenue of $2.4 million, up from $2.1 million, and profit of $310,000, up from $185,000 a year earlier. The directors have countered with a 2% offer.

Union representatives want to inspect the full final accounts before talks, arguing the figures prove the claim is affordable. Managing Director Priya Nair must decide between granting 6%, costing the business an extra $96,000 a year, and holding to 2%, costing $32,000 and releasing funds for a kiln replacement. The annual wage bill is $1.6 million.

questions.question_text: Define 'final accounts'.
questions.model_answer: Final accounts are the financial statements a business prepares at the end of an accounting period to show its profit, revenue and financial position, helping stakeholders judge performance [2].

knowledge_max_2: Statements prepared at the end of the accounting period
Show profit, revenue and financial position to stakeholders

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the Clay & Ceramics Union would want to see Wexcombe Pottery Ltd's final accounts.
questions.model_answer: First, the union wants to see whether the business can afford the 6% claim [k]. Profit rose to $310,000 on revenue of $2.4 million, so members argue the accounts prove the case for higher pay [app]. Second, the union uses the accounts to judge job security [k]. If profit fell back towards $185,000 or expenses spiked, jobs and future rises could be at risk, shaping whether to press for 6% or accept the $32,000 offer [app].

knowledge_max_2: Judge whether the business can afford the pay claim
Assess job security and the basis for negotiating
application_max_2: Reference to profit $310,000 (up from $185,000) and revenue $2.4 million
Reference to the 6% claim versus the 2% offer ($32,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the directors might face if they agree to the 6% claim.
questions.model_answer: First, agreeing the claim raises wage costs [k]. The extra $96,000 a year would come from profit of $310,000, leaving only about $214,000 before tax [app]. This squeezes the owners' return and could force price rises, risking orders from price-sensitive retailers [an]. Second, the claim absorbs funds for the kiln replacement [k]. The 2% offer costs $32,000, but 6% costs $96,000, a difference of $64,000 [app]. Without the new kiln, output and quality at Stokeham could deteriorate, hurting delivery reliability and customer trust [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher wage costs reduce profit and flexibility
Removes funds earmarked for investment (kiln)
application_max_2: Reference to $96,000 a year against the $1.6 million wage bill
Reference to profit $310,000 and 2% offer costing $32,000 / kiln replacement
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower retained profit to price rises to lost orders
Chain from no kiln to lower output and quality to lost customers

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should accept the 6% pay claim? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Granting the 6% claim would reward workers after a strong year [k]. It costs $96,000 a year, and with profit of $310,000 the business could pay it while keeping about $214,000, improving morale across all 58 workers and cutting the risk of strikes [app]. Better motivation could lift output and reduce labour turnover at the workshop, protecting revenue of $2.4 million [an]. However, the 6% claim absorbs the funds needed for the kiln replacement, unlike the 2% offer costing $32,000 [k]. Accepting 6% would also set a precedent the business cannot afford if profit falls back towards $185,000 [app]. Sustained higher wages could force price rises that lose customers to rivals, eroding the very profit that makes the claim affordable [an]. Overall, I think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should hold to the 2% offer plus a one-off profit-linked bonus [eval]. Profit did improve, but the full claim would commit about 31% of last year's profit to permanent extra wages when a cheaper deal funds both motivation and the kiln [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Granting improves morale / cuts risk of industrial action
6% removes kiln investment funds and sets a precedent
application_max_2: Reference to $96,000 a year and profit $310,000 / about $214,000 remaining
Reference to 2% offer costing $32,000 and profit possibly falling back to $185,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from morale to output and labour turnover to protected revenue
Chain from wage precedent to price rises to lost customers
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (2% plus bonus rather than full 6%)
Weighs both options with stem figures ($96,000 vs $32,000; 31% of profit)

scenario_stem:
Aldergate Cycle Works Plc manufactures and sells bicycles across Country X from its Denham factory, employing 340 people, and is listed on the Country X Stock Exchange with about 420 shareholders. For the year just ended, revenue was $24 million and profit was $2.6 million on capital employed of $18.6 million, a return on capital employed of 14%, up from 11% two years ago.

The board plans a $2.2 million assembly hall. Under Option A, it pays an unchanged 6c dividend on the 10 million shares in issue, costing $600,000, leaving $2.0 million from profit; the $200,000 shortfall would be borrowed at 9% interest. Under Option B, the dividend is cut to 4c, costing $400,000, and the hall is funded entirely from retained profit.

questions.question_text: Define 'dividend'.
questions.model_answer: A dividend is a payment made by a company to its shareholders out of profits, usually expressed per share held, as a return on their investment [2].

knowledge_max_2: Payment made to shareholders out of profits
Usually expressed per share; a return on shareholders' investment

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why shareholders would use the final accounts of Aldergate Cycle Works Plc.
questions.model_answer: First, shareholders use the accounts to judge whether the profit can support dividends [k]. Profit of $2.6 million covers the unchanged 6c dividend of $600,000, and ROCE of 14%, up from 11% two years ago, signals the business is using its capital well [app]. Second, shareholders use the accounts to assess the risk and growth prospects of their investment [k]. With revenue of $24 million and capital employed of $18.6 million, and the board planning a $2.2 million assembly hall, investors can judge future returns and decide between the 6c and 4c dividend options [app].

knowledge_max_2: Judge ability to pay dividends / profitability of the business
Assess risk and growth prospects before investing
application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.6 million, 6c/$600,000 dividend and ROCE 14% vs 11%
Reference to revenue $24 million, capital employed $18.6 million, $2.2 million hall

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Aldergate of funding the assembly hall from retained profit rather than borrowing.
questions.model_answer: First, funding from retained profit avoids interest charges [k]. Option B retains the full $2.2 million after a $400,000 dividend, whereas Option A leaves only $2.0 million and borrows $200,000 at 9%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [app]. Avoiding that cost directly improves profit and frees up cash for tooling and maintenance in the new hall [an]. Second, retained profit avoids new debt and keeps control with existing shareholders [k]. Cutting the dividend to 4c funds the hall without loans or security, and shareholders keep ownership of a business whose ROCE is already 14% [app]. Lower debt levels reduce financial risk and protect independence, supporting the share price on the Country X Stock Exchange [an].

knowledge_max_2: Avoids interest cost on borrowed funds
Avoids new debt / keeps control with existing shareholders
application_max_2: Reference to Option B retaining the full $2.2 million after a $400,000 dividend
Reference to Option A: $2.0 million left, $200,000 borrowed at 9% = about $18,000 a year
analysis_max_2: Chain from avoided interest to higher profit and freer cash
Chain from avoiding debt to lower financial risk and independence

questions.question_text: Do you think shareholders should approve the 4c dividend? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Approving 4c would give the board $2.2 million to build the hall without borrowing [k]. Shareholders give up $200,000 of income, with the dividend falling from 6c to 4c on the 10 million shares in issue, but Aldergate avoids about $18,000 a year of interest and retains full independence [app]. A bigger, more efficient hall should lift output and revenue beyond $24 million, supporting future dividends and ROCE holding above 14% [an]. However, many shareholders rely on dividend income, and cutting the payout by a third may prompt some to sell, depressing the share price [k]. Others would prefer Option A's unchanged $600,000 payout with a modest $200,000 loan, accepting $18,000 annual interest to keep income stable [app]. Heavy selling could signal weak confidence and push the share price down, wiping out the income slowdown [an]. Overall, I think shareholders should approve the 4c dividend [eval]. It funds a $2.2 million hall, avoids debt, and reinvests profit when ROCE is rising, a price worth paying provided the board publishes clear targets for restoring dividends once the hall opens [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Approving gives $2.2 million without borrowing
Some shareholders rely on income; a cut may press the share price down
application_max_2: Reference to $200,000 income loss and $18,000 a year interest avoided
Reference to Option A: 6c plus a $200,000 loan at 9%; 10 million shares
analysis_max_2: Chain from hall investment to output and revenue to future dividends
Chain from heavy shareholder selling to weaker share price
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified approval of the 4c dividend
Weighs both options with stem figures ($400,000 vs $600,000; $2.2 million hall)

scenario_stem:
Ternhill Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago, which makes cheese and butter and supplies 14 regional supermarkets. It employs 46 staff and has applied to Country X Bank for a $400,000 loan to buy three refrigerated delivery vans. Last year it reported revenue of $5.1 million and profit of $420,000.

The statement of financial position shows current assets of $980,000, including inventories of $350,000 and debtors of $520,000, against current liabilities of $600,000. The current ratio has fallen to 1.63 from 1.9 two years ago, and the acid test ratio has fallen to 1.05 from 1.3. Cash at bank is $110,000 and the loan application is with the credit manager this week.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due, using cash or assets that can quickly be turned into cash [2].

knowledge_max_2: Ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due
Using cash or assets quickly convertible to cash

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Country X Bank would examine Ternhill Dairy Ltd's statement of financial position before granting the loan.
questions.model_answer: First, the bank wants to judge whether short-term debts can be paid [k]. Current assets of $980,000 against current liabilities of $600,000 give a current ratio of 1.63, down from 1.9 two years ago, which tells the bank Ternhill has some cushion but a weakening one [app]. Second, the bank wants to know what can be turned into cash quickly [k]. With inventories of $350,000 the acid test ratio is 1.05, down from 1.3, and cash is only $110,000, so the bank would probe the $520,000 of debtors to see whether supermarkets pay on time [app].

knowledge_max_2: Judge ability to pay short-term debts
Assess how much is quickly convertible to cash
application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.63 vs 1.9; current assets $980,000 vs current liabilities $600,000
Reference to acid test 1.05 vs 1.3; inventories $350,000, debtors $520,000, cash $110,000

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio and the acid test ratio to judge Ternhill's ability to repay the loan.
questions.model_answer: First, ratios are a snapshot at one date [k]. Ternhill's current ratio of 1.63 and acid test ratio of 1.05 held at the year end, but a single late supermarket payment or a big stock delivery could change both quickly, so the figures may flatter the business on the day the $400,000 loan is decided [app]. Liquidity could be materially weaker exactly when the first instalments fall due [an]. Second, ratios ignore the quality of what the business owns [k]. Of the $980,000 of current assets, $350,000 is inventories and $520,000 is debtors; slow-paying or defaulting supermarkets, or damaged stocks, would shrink the real acid test well below 1.05 [app]. The bank could lend on the strength of figures that evaporate once debtors and inventories are properly valued [an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios are a snapshot at one date; figures change quickly
Ratios ignore the quality of assets (stock and debtors may be impaired)
application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.63 and acid test 1.05 at year end
Reference to inventories $350,000 and debtors $520,000 of $980,000 current assets
analysis_max_2: Chain from year-end snapshot to weaker instalment-date liquidity
Chain from impaired stock or debtors to an overstated acid test

questions.question_text: Do you think Country X Bank should grant the $400,000 loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Ternhill is profitable, with profit of $420,000 almost covering the $400,000 loan in a single year [k]. Revenue of $5.1 million and supply deals with 14 regional supermarkets suggest steady cash generation, and three refrigerated vans would cut spoilage and secure deliveries, supporting future sales [app]. Stronger distribution could widen margins and lift profit further, improving the bank's repayment prospects across the term of the loan [an]. However, liquidity is weakening: the current ratio has fallen from 1.9 to 1.63, the acid test from 1.3 to 1.05, cash is only $110,000 and debtors are $520,000 — more than half of current assets [k]. Granting cash before debtors are collected could leave Ternhill unable to meet early instalments, especially if one supermarket pays late [app]. A rushed approval could turn a good customer into an overdraft problem, adding risk and cost to the bank with no extra margin [an]. Overall, I think Country X Bank should grant the loan, but in staged instalments linked to milestones, with vans delivered and debtors collected down to agreed limits [eval]. The profit and revenue justify supporting the business, yet the weakening acid test and $110,000 cash balance demand controls rather than one upfront payout [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Profitable business; loan is close to one year of profit
Weakening current ratio, acid test and cash position
application_max_2: Reference to revenue $5.1 million, profit $420,000 and 14 supermarkets
Reference to cash $110,000, debtors $520,000, current ratio 1.63, acid test 1.05
analysis_max_2: Chain from new vans to lower spoilage and stronger sales to easier repayment
Chain from rushed approval to overdraft pressure and added risk
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to lend in stages
Weighs both sides with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd is a family-run private limited company in Country X, founded 15 years ago, supplying roofing, insulation and timber to the construction trade. It employs 28 staff. A new customer, Hollowbrook Homes Ltd, a housing developer, wants to buy $180,000 of materials for a 24-house estate and asks for 60 days to pay.

Hollowbrook Homes' latest accounts show revenue of $6.4 million, profit of $250,000, current assets of $550,000 including inventories of $250,000, and current liabilities of $500,000, giving a current ratio of 1.1 and an acid test ratio of 0.6. Hollowbrook has also been slow to pay its existing suppliers. Wicklow must decide by Friday between granting 60-day credit or insisting on 30-day terms, risking the order to a rival merchant.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade credit'.
questions.model_answer: Trade credit is an arrangement allowing a customer to receive goods immediately and pay the supplier after an agreed period, such as 30 or 60 days [2].

knowledge_max_2: Goods received before payment
Payment made after an agreed period such as 30 or 60 days

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd would want to see Hollowbrook Homes Ltd's accounts before offering trade credit.
questions.model_answer: First, the accounts show whether Hollowbrook can pay [k]. Current assets of $550,000 against current liabilities of $500,000 give a current ratio of 1.1 and an acid test ratio of 0.6, so quick funds are thin for settling a $180,000 invoice [app]. Second, the accounts show whether the order is reasonable for the customer's size [k]. Revenue of $6.4 million and profit of $250,000 against a $180,000 order means the deal equals 72% of annual profit, so Wicklow must judge whether the margin justifies the exposure [app].

knowledge_max_2: Assess ability to pay (liquidity)
Assess order size relative to the customer's resources
application_max_2: Reference to current ratio 1.1, acid test 0.6, current assets $550,000 vs current liabilities $500,000
Reference to $180,000 order = 72% of $250,000 profit on revenue of $6.4 million

questions.question_text: Explain two risks to Wicklow of granting 60-day credit.
questions.model_answer: First, Wicklow faces late or non-payment [k]. Hollowbrook's acid test of 0.6 and inventories of $250,000, nearly half its current assets, show cash is tight and it is already slow paying existing suppliers, so the $180,000 could sit unpaid well beyond 60 days [app]. Wicklow would then lack cash for its own stock and wages, possibly needing costly overdraft borrowing [an]. Second, a single large customer raises dependence [k]. The $180,000 order equals 72% of Hollowbrook's $250,000 profit, so one default or insolvency would be a heavy blow to a 28-staff merchant [app]. Losing that sum could wipe out Wicklow's margin on the whole estate deal and strain relations with its own suppliers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Risk of late payment or default
Dependence on one large customer
application_max_2: Reference to acid test 0.6, inventories $250,000 (nearly half of current assets) and slow payment of suppliers
Reference to $180,000 = 72% of $250,000 profit; 28 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from late payment to Wicklow cash strain and overdraft costs
Chain from one default to lost margin and supplier strain

questions.question_text: Do you think Wicklow Builders Merchants Ltd should grant the 60-day credit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Granting 60-day credit could win a $180,000 order for a 24-house estate and open a long-term relationship with a growing developer [k]. Hollowbrook is profitable at $250,000 on revenue of $6.4 million, and the deal equals 72% of its profit, so losing it to a rival merchant would hand over valuable future estate business [app]. Securing the account could bring regular orders and steady sales without new advertising spend [an]. However, Hollowbrook's liquidity is weak: acid test 0.6, current ratio 1.1, inventories of $250,000 and a record of slow payment to existing suppliers [k]. If payment slips beyond 60 days, Wicklow faces a cash gap of $180,000 on top of its own commitments, risking its ability to pay suppliers and staff [app]. One bad debt could erase months of Wicklow's margin, and repeated chasing strains the relationship the deal was meant to build [an]. Overall, I think Wicklow should not grant 60 days on the current terms [eval]; it should insist on 30-day terms, or staged payments with a deposit, because the acid test of 0.6 and the slow payment history do not justify open-ended 60-day credit, however attractive the order looks [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Winning the order builds a relationship and future business
Weak liquidity and slow payment history make 60 days risky
application_max_2: Reference to $180,000 order, $250,000 profit, 72% of profit, 24-house estate
Reference to acid test 0.6, current ratio 1.1, inventories $250,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from winning the account to regular future orders
Chain from late payment to a cash gap and bad-debt risk
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (30-day terms or staged payments instead)
Weighs both options with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Stonemere Haulage Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, based at the Kinwell depot and the Northgate satellite yard, running 9 lorries for food and retail clients. It employs 34 drivers and warehouse staff. The government has announced grants covering 40% of the cost of electric trucks, provided applicants show two consecutive profitable years and create 3 new jobs per truck purchased.

Stonemere wants to buy 3 electric trucks at $160,000 each, totalling $480,000. Retained profit stands at $500,000 and the last two years produced profits of $175,000 and $210,000. The grant would contribute $192,000, leaving Stonemere to fund $288,000, but accepting it would oblige Stonemere to keep 9 new drivers for 3 years, publish its accounts annually and meet government reporting requirements.

questions.question_text: Define 'retained profit'.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit is the profit left in the business after tax and shareholder dividends, kept in the business to reinvest in growth or fund future plans [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit remaining after tax and dividends
Kept in the business for reinvestment or future plans

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the government agency would want to see Stonemere Haulage Ltd's accounts before approving the grant.
questions.model_answer: First, the agency must verify the two-year profit rule [k]. Stonemere's profits of $175,000 and $210,000 in consecutive years meet the eligibility test, and retained profit of $500,000 confirms the business is viable [app]. Second, the agency must judge whether the promised jobs will last [k]. Accounts showing steady profit and a $500,000 cushion help the agency assess whether Stonemere can pay nine drivers for three years, not just create paper jobs [app].

knowledge_max_2: Verify two consecutive profitable years (eligibility)
Assess ability to sustain the jobs for 3 years
application_max_2: Reference to profits of $175,000 and $210,000 in consecutive years
Reference to retained profit of $500,000 and nine drivers kept for three years

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks to Stonemere of accepting the grant.
questions.model_answer: First, the grant binds Stonemere to keep 9 drivers for three years [k]. If demand falls, Stonemere must still pay nine wages although retained profit of $500,000 might otherwise fund maintenance or marketing [app]. This shrinks flexibility and could push the business into losses if a major client leaves [an]. Second, accepting means publishing accounts annually [k]. Clients and rivals would see that profit was $210,000 last year, weakening Stonemere's hand in price negotiations [app]. Visible margins invite tougher customer demands and higher wage claims, eroding much of the $192,000 benefit over three years [an].

knowledge_max_2: Three-year, nine-job obligation reduces flexibility
Accounts must be published annually; loss of confidentiality
application_max_2: Reference to 9 drivers kept for 3 years against $500,000 retained profit
Reference to published profit of $210,000 and grant value of $192,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from rigid wages to losses if demand falls
Chain from published margins to tougher client negotiations

questions.question_text: Do you think Stonemere Haulage Ltd should apply for the government grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Applying secures $192,000 of the $480,000 truck cost, cutting Stonemere's own funding to $288,000 [k]. With retained profit of $500,000, the business keeps $212,000 in reserve for repairs and working capital, healthier than spending $480,000 outright, and three electric trucks fit the fleet's efficiency plans [app]. Lower operating costs per kilometre and contracts won on green credentials could lift profit beyond $210,000 a year, covering the grant obligations comfortably [an]. However, accepting ties Stonemere to keep 9 drivers for 3 years even through downturns, and its accounts must be published annually, exposing margins to clients and rivals [k]. Stonemere could instead fund $480,000 entirely from retained profit, leaving just $20,000, keeping full control and confidentiality with no government reporting [app]. Losing privacy could cost more than $192,000 over three years if clients demand price cuts on that evidence [an]. Overall, I think Stonemere should apply for the grant [eval], because $192,000 is 40% of the purchase price and preserving $212,000 of liquidity outweighs the publication risk, but only if it is confident of retaining the 9 drivers and handling the extra reporting for three years [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Secures $192,000 (40%) of the truck cost
Binding obligations: 9 jobs, 3 years, published accounts
application_max_2: Reference to $288,000 own funding, $500,000 retained profit, $212,000 reserve
Reference to paying $480,000 outright leaving just $20,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from a green fleet to lower costs and new contracts
Chain from published accounts to price pressure from clients
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to apply
Weighs both options with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Halcyon Reef Resorts Ltd runs three eco-resorts on the Country X coast and employs 210 staff. Comparing the last two years, revenue rose from $9.6 million to $10.4 million, but gross profit margin fell from 52% to 47% and profit fell from $840,000 to $720,000, a drop of $120,000. The current ratio held at 1.8 in both years and occupancy averaged 78%.

Managing Directors Aisha Bellocq and Tom Reyes disagree on the response. Option A raises room rates from $145 to $154, a rise of $9, to recover the margin. Option B keeps rates unchanged and cuts operating costs, mainly by re-tendering laundry and kitchen contracts, saving $120,000 a year but with some risk to service consistency. They have asked analysts to compare the accounts over the two years.

questions.question_text: Define 'ratio analysis'.
questions.model_answer: Ratio analysis is the use of financial ratios, such as gross profit margin, return on capital employed and the current ratio, to assess a business's performance and financial position, often compared over time [2].

knowledge_max_2: Using financial ratios to assess performance and financial position
Comparisons over time or against other businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why comparing the accounts over two years is useful to managers.
questions.model_answer: First, two years of ratios reveal trends that a single year cannot [k]. Revenue rising from $9.6 million to $10.4 million looks healthy on its own, but the gross profit margin falling from 52% to 47% shows growth is being bought with weaker pricing or higher input costs [app]. Second, trend analysis helps locate the problem precisely [k]. A current ratio steady at 1.8 alongside falling profit shows liquidity is fine, so managers should attack costs or pricing, and the profit drop of $120,000 matches the projected $120,000 saving exactly [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reveals trends that a single year cannot
Locates whether problems are cost, price or liquidity
application_max_2: Reference to revenue $9.6 million to $10.4 million; gross profit margin 52% to 47%
Reference to current ratio steady at 1.8; profit fall of $120,000 matching the $120,000 saving

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of comparing Halcyon's ratios over just two years.
questions.model_answer: First, two years is a short window and may catch one-off events [k]. Halcyon's profit fell from $840,000 to $720,000 partly because of higher laundry and kitchen costs, which the $120,000 saving would reverse, so the 47% margin may understate underlying performance [app]. Judging on a single cost shock could push directors into rushed rate rises or cuts that harm guests [an]. Second, ratios ignore qualitative factors [k]. Occupancy of 78% shows rooms are selling, but guest satisfaction, staff morale and brand reputation, all affected by Option B's service-consistency risk, sit outside the numbers [app]. Cutting the wrong contracts could save $120,000 yet damage the experience that drives occupancy and revenue of $10.4 million [an].

knowledge_max_2: Short window; one-off events distort the picture
Ratios ignore qualitative factors (service, morale, brand)
application_max_2: Reference to profit $840,000 to $720,000; 47% margin; $120,000 saving
Reference to occupancy 78% and revenue of $10.4 million
analysis_max_2: Chain from a short window to rushed, harmful decisions
Chain from blunt cost cuts to damaged occupancy and revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Halcyon Reef Resorts Ltd should choose Option B rather than Option A? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises rates from $145 to $154, a $9 increase, restoring revenue from existing guests without restructuring operations [k]. With occupancy at 78%, even a modest rise lifts revenue across three resorts, but it may deter price-sensitive holidaymakers already facing higher costs elsewhere [app]. If even 5% of guests defect, the lost contribution could erase the extra $9 a night and push occupancy below break-even [an]. Option B keeps rates at $145 and cuts costs by $120,000 a year, exactly the profit lost, by re-tendering laundry and kitchen contracts [k]. This attacks the problem directly and protects the $145 rate that keeps the resorts competitive, provided service standards are monitored closely [app]. Well-run contracts could restore profit towards $840,000 without touching price or occupancy [an]. Overall, I think Halcyon should choose Option B, with strict service-level monitoring [eval]; it exactly offsets the $120,000 profit fall and avoids demand risk at 78% occupancy, whereas Option A remains a useful fallback if service complaints rise after the switch [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A restores revenue but risks demand at 78% occupancy
Option B targets the cost cause and protects price and occupancy
application_max_2: Reference to $145 to $154 ($9) and occupancy 78% at three resorts
Reference to $120,000 saving equalling the profit lost; profit back towards $840,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from a rate rise to guest defections and lower occupancy
Chain from cost re-tendering to protected price and margin recovery
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation for Option B with safeguards
Weighs both options with stem figures

scenario_stem:
Wrenfield Cider Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing apple cider, with revenue of $4.1 million, a gross profit margin of 39%, ROCE of 11% and a current ratio of 1.7. Its board is considering buying its smaller rival, Fenwick Orchards Ltd, whose accounts show revenue of $3.2 million, a gross profit margin of 44%, ROCE of 16% on capital employed of $1.6 million, helped by a one-off land sale contributing $90,000 of profit, and a current ratio of 1.4. Fenwick values inventories using a different method and its figures are already 12 months old.

Fenwick is asking $2.6 million. The board compares the two sets of accounts and debates whether the higher ratios prove Fenwick is the better business. Directors know ratio analysis has limitations and want wider evidence before committing to the purchase.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio is a liquidity ratio that compares a business's current assets with its current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities [2].

knowledge_max_2: Compares current assets with current liabilities
Calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Fenwick's higher ratios might not prove it is the better buy.
questions.model_answer: First, one-off items can flatter a single year's ratios [k]. Fenwick's 16% ROCE was helped by a $90,000 one-off land sale, so underlying profit is nearer $166,000; $2.6 million is more than fifteen years of that recurring profit [app]. Second, different accounting policies distort comparisons [k]. Fenwick values inventories on a different basis and its figures are already 12 months old, so its 44% gross profit margin and 1.4 current ratio are not directly comparable with Wrenfield's 39% and 1.7 accounts [app].

knowledge_max_2: One-off items can distort a single year's ratios
Different accounting policies undermine comparability

Reference to Fenwick's inventory method and figures being 12 months old; 44% vs 39% gross profit margin; 1.4 vs 1.7 current ratio

questions.question_text: Explain two other checks Wrenfield should make before buying Fenwick.
questions.model_answer: First, Wrenfield should inspect Fenwick's physical assets and stock [k]. A current ratio of 1.4 tells nothing about condition; ageing cider, obsolete labels or tired bottling kit would force post-purchase write-downs, eroding the $2.6 million price [app]. Overstated assets would mean Wrenfield pays for value that no longer exists [an]. Second, Wrenfield should review Fenwick's customer contracts and forward orders [k]. Revenue of $3.2 million and a 44% gross profit margin mean little if pub and retail accounts are uncontracted, paying late, or reflecting a fading local cider trend captured in the 12-month-old figures [app]. Losing a key account after completion would cut the profit base that justified the price [an].

knowledge_max_2: Inspect physical assets and stock quality
Review customer contracts and forward orders
application_max_2: Reference to the current ratio of 1.4 and the $2.6 million price
Reference to revenue of $3.2 million at a 44% gross profit margin and 12-month-old figures

Chain from lost accounts to a collapsed profit rationale

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenfield Cider Ltd should buy Fenwick Orchards Ltd for $2.6 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying would remove a rival and add $3.2 million of revenue at a 44% gross profit margin to Wrenfield's $4.1 million, 39% operation [k]. Even with the $90,000 one-off stripped out, leaving nearer $166,000 of recurring profit, synergies in buying apples, bottling and distribution could lift both margins and make the $2.6 million pay back faster [app]. If Wrenfield shares distribution routes and negotiates bulk supply, the deal could raise its own 39% margin towards Fenwick's 44% [an]. However, Fenwick's figures are 12 months old, inventories are valued differently, and its 16% ROCE rests partly on the $90,000 land sale [k]. Paying $2.6 million on unaudited, mismatched evidence risks overpaying by a wide margin, with limited recourse after completion [app]. A bad deal could tie up Wrenfield's cash for years, weaken its own current ratio of 1.7 and leave it exposed to poor harvests [an]. Overall, I think Wrenfield should not buy Fenwick at $2.6 million on the current evidence [eval]; it should renegotiate the price or commission updated, adjusted accounts and a stock audit first, since $2.6 million, more than fifteen years of recurring profit near $166,000, cannot be justified on a flattering single year [eval].

scenario_stem:
Garrow Fresh Fish Ltd is a private limited company in Country X supplying smoked and fresh fish to retail stores in the Northgate region. It employs 37 staff. Last year it reported revenue of $3.6 million and profit of $320,000, but cash at the bank is only $85,000 and debtors stand at $640,000 after several customers stretched their payment terms.

Its largest customer, Regional Stores Group, offers a 2-year exclusive contract worth $900,000 a year but demands payment after 90 days and a 4% price cut, worth $36,000 a year. Taking the order would add about $225,000 of unpaid invoices at any time, more than two and a half times the cash at bank. Garrow must decide by the end of this month.

questions.question_text: Outline the difference between profit and cash.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the surplus of revenue over costs shown in the income statement, while cash is the actual money available in the bank to pay bills; a business can be profitable yet run out of cash [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit = revenue minus costs, shown in the income statement
Cash = money actually available; a profitable firm can still lack cash

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit and cash differ for Garrow Fresh Fish Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, sales on credit are booked as revenue before cash arrives [k]. Garrow's profit of $320,000 includes sales the income statement counts even though debtors already stand at $640,000, far above the $85,000 cash at bank [app]. Second, fish is bought, processed and delivered before customers pay [k]. Cash leaves the bank for suppliers and wages weeks before receipts arrive, and the $900,000 contract on 90-day terms would add about $225,000 of unpaid invoices at any time [app].

knowledge_max_2: Credit sales are recorded as revenue before cash arrives
Payments to suppliers and wages leave before customer receipts arrive
application_max_2: Reference to profit $320,000 vs debtors $640,000 vs cash $85,000
Reference to $900,000 contract at 90 days adding about $225,000 of unpaid invoices

questions.question_text: Explain two risks to Garrow of accepting the 90-day payment terms.
questions.model_answer: First, 90-day terms would strain working capital [k]. The contract adds about $225,000 of unpaid invoices, more than two and a half times the cash at bank of $85,000, while fish suppliers still need paying, so Garrow may need an overdraft whose interest eats into the $320,000 profit [app]. Sustained strain could force Garrow to delay its own payments and damage supplier trust [an]. Second, dependence on one dominant customer is risky [k]. Regional Stores Group demands 90-day payment plus a 4% price cut worth $36,000 a year, and an exclusive 2-year deal would concentrate Garrow's sales on a single buyer [app]. If that customer delisted Garrow or paid late, the $900,000 revenue stream could weaken suddenly, endangering the 37 jobs and margins across the wider business [an].

knowledge_max_2: Working capital and cash-flow strain
Dependence on one dominant customer
application_max_2: Reference to about $225,000 added invoices vs $85,000 cash; $640,000 existing debtors; $320,000 profit
Reference to 4% cut worth $36,000 a year; exclusive 2-year deal; $900,000 revenue
analysis_max_2: Chain from cash strain to overdraft costs and delayed payments
Chain from customer concentration to sudden revenue risk and job losses

questions.question_text: Do you think Garrow Fresh Fish Ltd should accept the Regional Stores Group contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting would secure $900,000 a year of revenue for two years, a quarter of last year's $3.6 million, and guarantee shelf space in Regional Stores Group's outlets [k]. The 4% price cut costs $36,000 a year, but the exclusive deal should still lift total revenue and use of the 37 staff more fully, and repeat regional exposure builds the brand [app]. Steady two-year demand would support investment in packing and cold storage, widening Garrow's margin on all its sales [an]. However, 90-day terms add about $225,000 of unpaid invoices on top of existing debtors of $640,000, against cash of just $85,000 [k]. Accepting as drafted could leave Garrow cash-negative within months, unable to pay fish suppliers and risking the credit it needs to trade [app]. Contribution margins would also be capped for two years with no room to reprice [an]. Overall, I think Garrow should accept the contract only if the 90-day terms are renegotiated to 60 days or backed by a bank overdraft [eval]. At 90 days unamended the cash strain outweighs the revenue gain, but with credit secured the $36,000 concession is easily outweighed by two years of guaranteed demand [eval].

Adds about $225,000 of invoices on $640,000 of debtors against $85,000 cash

Reference to 37 staff, $640,000 debtors and $85,000 cash

scenario_stem:
Amberfield Fabrics Plc is listed on the Country X Stock Exchange and weaves shirting and suiting fabrics for fashion retailers from its Redmile mill, employing 480 staff. To fund $3 million of new weaving machinery, the board plans a share issue, and under Country X rules the accounts must be published so investors can judge the offer fairly.

Option A is to publish full accounts with a detailed prospectus, showing revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a gross profit margin of 34% and a dividend of 5c per share on the 25 million shares in issue. Option B is to publish only the minimum required audited statements, keeping margin detail and customer information confidential, but risking a weak response from investors.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'published accounts'.
questions.model_answer: Published accounts are the financial statements a limited company must make publicly available, showing its performance and financial position, so shareholders, lenders, employees, customers and the government can assess them [2].

knowledge_max_2: Financial statements a limited company must make publicly available
Used by shareholders, lenders, employees, customers and the government

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Amberfield Fabrics Plc's accounts are published.
questions.model_answer: First, publication is a legal requirement for a listed company [k]. Under Country X rules, a Plc on the Stock Exchange raising $3 million through a share issue must publish audited accounts so the offer is transparent to investors [app]. Second, publication lets stakeholders assess the business [k]. Investors can see revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a 34% gross profit margin and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares ($1.25 million), judging whether the new machinery justifies subscribing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Legal requirement for a listed Plc
Transparency so stakeholders can assess the business
application_max_2: Reference to $3 million share issue and Country X Stock Exchange rules
Reference to revenue $12 million, profit $1.5 million, 34% margin, 5c on 25 million shares = $1.25 million

questions.question_text: Explain two stakeholders, other than shareholders, who use Amberfield Fabrics Plc's published accounts and why.
questions.model_answer: First, employees use published accounts to judge job security and pay prospects [k]. With 480 staff at the Redmile mill and profit of $1.5 million on revenue of $12 million, the workforce can see the business is profitable and funded for new machinery, shaping wage negotiations and retention of skilled weavers [app]. If the accounts instead showed falling profit, staff could anticipate restructuring and plan accordingly [an]. Second, the government uses published accounts to assess tax and approve support [k]. Corporation tax on the $1.5 million profit is computed from these figures, and agencies licensing the machinery or granting support rely on the same audited numbers [app]. Accurate reporting funds public services and keeps Amberfield compliant, avoiding penalties and reputational damage [an].

knowledge_max_2: Employees use them to judge job security and pay
Government uses them to assess tax and approve grants or licences
application_max_2: Reference to 480 staff at the Redmile mill; profit $1.5 million on revenue of $12 million
Reference to corporation tax computed on $1.5 million profit and machinery licensing
analysis_max_2: Chain from visible profit to wage negotiations and retention
Chain from accurate reporting to compliance, public revenue and avoiding penalties

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfield Fabrics Plc should publish full accounts as part of the share issue prospectus? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Publishing full accounts gives investors the evidence to subscribe for the $3 million issue [k]. Transparent figures, showing revenue of $12 million, profit of $1.5 million, a gross profit margin of 34% and a 5c dividend on 25 million shares worth $1.25 million, build trust, improving uptake and reducing the risk the issue fails [app]. Strong disclosure could attract institutional investors, securing the weaving machinery sooner and lifting output, sales and the share price [an]. However, full disclosure exposes margins and cost structures to rivals [k]. Rivals could undercut Amberfield or poach customers once the 34% margin and $1.5 million profit are public, and customers may press for lower prices on that evidence [app]. The competitive damage could exceed the financing benefit, making Option B's minimum publication tempting despite a weaker investor response [an]. Overall, I think Amberfield should publish the full accounts [eval]. As a listed Plc it already publishes audited statements, and the $3 million issue needs investor confidence; margins on shirting fabrics are hard to hide in a public offer anyway, and the certainty of funding outweighs the extra visibility, though customer lists should stay confidential [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Full accounts give investors evidence and build trust
Full disclosure exposes margins and cost structures to rivals
application_max_2: Reference to revenue $12 million, profit $1.5 million, 34% margin, 5c dividend on 25 million shares ($1.25 million)
Reference to rivals or customers using published margins to undercut or renegotiate
analysis_max_2: Chain from disclosure to investor uptake to secured machinery and growth
Chain from visibility to price pressure and competitive damage
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to publish in full

scenario_stem:
Carrow Insulation Plc manufactures insulation boards for commercial buildings across Country X. Daljit Singh owns 40,000 of its 30 million shares. The accounts show revenue of $14 million, $15 million and $15.5 million over the last three years, while profit fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million and then $1.2 million. ROCE fell from 17% to 12% and then 8%, and the dividend has been cut from 6c to 2c per share.

The current ratio held steady at 1.6 and gross profit margin slipped from 33% to 31% and then 24%. Daljit is deciding whether to sell his shares now, when they trade well below last year's price, or hold and hope the new chief executive's turnaround plan, including plant modernisation and tighter cost control, restores returns.

questions.question_text: Define 'acid test ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio is a liquidity ratio measuring whether a business can pay its short-term debts from its most liquid assets, calculated as current assets minus inventories, divided by current liabilities [2].

knowledge_max_2: A liquidity ratio using the most liquid assets
Formula: (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Daljit Singh would compare Carrow Insulation Plc's accounts over three years before deciding to sell.
questions.model_answer: First, one year can flatter or alarm [k]. Profit of $1.2 million alone looks merely weak, but set against $2.4 million and $1.9 million in prior years it confirms a steady decline, with ROCE falling from 17% to 12% and then 8% over the same period [app]. Second, trends show whether the dividend is sustainable [k]. The dividend has been cut from 6c to 2c per share, so Daljit's income on 40,000 shares has fallen from $2,400 to $800 a year, and the three-year figures reveal whether this is a temporary dip or a structural decline [app].

knowledge_max_2: A single year can mislead; the trend shows direction
Reveals whether the dividend is sustainable
application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.4 million to $1.9 million to $1.2 million; ROCE 17% to 12% to 8%
Reference to dividend cut from 6c to 2c; income falling from $2,400 to $800 on 40,000 shares

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE alone to judge Carrow Insulation Plc's performance.
questions.model_answer: First, ROCE ignores liquidity completely [k]. Carrow's current ratio held at 1.6 across all three years, genuinely stable, but ROCE of 8% says nothing about whether cash or debtors are under strain underneath that figure [app]. A shareholder judging by ROCE alone could miss early warning signs that a steady 1.6 can still conceal [an]. Second, ROCE does not show where the decline comes from [k]. Revenue actually grew from $14 million to $15.5 million, yet the gross profit margin slid from 33% to 24%, growth at worse pricing rather than weak demand [app]. Blind to margin detail, ROCE could mislabel Carrow's problem as a market dip rather than a cost or pricing failure, misleading sell decisions [an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE ignores liquidity (current ratio steady at 1.6)
ROCE hides the source of decline (margin compression vs demand)
application_max_2: Reference to the current ratio holding at 1.6 in all three years and ROCE of 8%
Reference to revenue rising $14 million to $15.5 million while gross profit margin slid 33% to 24%
analysis_max_2: Chain from a ROCE-only view to missed liquidity stress
Chain from margin detail to a misdiagnosed problem

questions.question_text: Do you think Daljit Singh should sell his 40,000 shares? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Selling now crystallises the reality of a three-year slide: profit fell from $2.4 million to $1.9 million and then $1.2 million, ROCE from 17% to 8%, and the dividend from 6c to 2c, cutting Daljit's income from $2,400 to $800 a year [k]. Waiting for the turnaround risks further losses if plant modernisation and cost control underperform, and the share price already trades well below last year's level [app]. Selling frees cash to redeploy into higher-yielding investments while the margin trend of 33% to 24% remains unproven [an]. However, holding has merit [k]. Carrow's current ratio has stayed at 1.6 for three years and revenue grew from $14 million to $15.5 million, showing demand is intact under a new chief executive with a modernisation plan [app]. If he restores the gross profit margin from 24% towards 33%, ROCE could recover towards double digits and the share price would reward patient holders [an]. Overall, I think Daljit should sell his 40,000 shares [eval]. Three consecutive years of falling profit, ROCE and dividend, with no turnaround evidence yet delivered, make holding speculation rather than investment; he can re-enter if the plan shows two quarters of margin recovery, but discipline says sell now at the current weak price [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Selling crystallises losses and cuts risk exposure
Holding has merit if the turnaround delivers
application_max_2: Reference to profit $2.4 million to $1.9 million to $1.2 million; ROCE 17% to 8%; dividend 6c to 2c; income $2,400 to $800
Reference to current ratio steady at 1.6, revenue $14 million to $15.5 million and margin 33% to 24%
analysis_max_2: Chain from an unproven margin trend to a weak share price
Chain from a successful turnaround to recovering ROCE and price
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation to sell
Weighs both options with stem figures
